\chapter{Hablara --- the Form for Supposing}
\label{ch:hablara}
\hlchaptermodality{206}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build the supposing form of any verb from its they-past.}

I can build the supposing form of any verb from its they-past.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablara]{hablara}

\label{lesson:ES-C56-hablara}



\begin{quote}
Give the \emph{they} past of \emph{hablar}, \emph{comer} and \emph{vivir}. (\emph{Hablaron, comieron, vivieron}.)

You were told those would be used twice. This is the second time.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: swap the ending}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Take the \emph{they} past. Swap \emph{-ron} for \emph{-ra}.}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{they past} & \textbf{supposing} \\
\midrule
hablaron & \textbf{hablara} \\
comieron & \textbf{comiera} \\
vivieron & \textbf{viviera} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{No verb in Spanish changes its stem here} — a stronger guarantee than almost anything else in the language. The one thing the swap does not carry is an accent: \emph{habl\textbf{á}ramos}, \emph{tuvi\textbf{é}ramos}. The stem is untouched; only the mark moves.

The reason is worth a moment: every irregularity these verbs had was already spent in the preterite. Because this form is carved out of that one, it \textbf{inherits the irregularity instead of inventing new irregularity}. A tense built on a broken form comes out perfectly regular.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Hablara\emph{ did not start out as supposing.\textbf{}}}}

In Latin this ending was a plain statement about the past: \emph{amāveram}, \textbf{I had loved}. It slid from \emph{what had happened} to \emph{what did not}, which is a short journey — both sit outside the present, and only one is real.

(\emph{Hablar}'s Latin ancestor was \textbf{deponent}, so Spanish built \emph{hablara} on the pattern rather than inheriting it. The ending carried over, not the word.)

Spanish also has a second form for exactly this job — \emph{hablase} — and that one \textbf{did} come from a Latin subjunctive. Two different Latin tenses walked into the same modern meaning. You will meet \emph{-se} in reading; you never have to produce it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hablaron $\to$ hablara}
  \item \emph{comieron $\to$ comiera}, \emph{vivieron $\to$ viviera}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you start from? (The \emph{\textbf{they}} \textbf{past}.) What do you swap? (\emph{\textbf{-ron}} for \emph{\textbf{-ra}}.)

How many verbs change their stem? (\textbf{None} — the breaking already happened somewhere else.) And what does move? (The \textbf{accent}, in the \emph{nosotros} form.)
\end{tcolorbox}
